stem: A bank says its new dashboard delivers 'business intelligence'. In which of the course's three senses is the word 'intelligence' being used?
choices: Human-like — the dashboard could pass for a person in conversation
Advantageous information of strategic or tactical value
A clever solution method for a hard computational problem
General intelligence across every task a human can do
explanation: Business Intelligence uses 'intelligence' the way military intelligence does: extracted information of tactical value. The 'I' in AI means human-like; the 'I' in Computational Intelligence means an optimal solution method for a complex problem.

stem: Turing's imitation game tests which of the three senses of the 'I' in 'AI'?
choices: Human-like — quality of interaction good enough that you cannot tell machine from person
Advantageous information, as in military or business intelligence
Optimal solution path, as in computational or digital intelligence
Self-awareness, as in the consciousness marker
explanation: Turing's test is purely the human-like sense: a system passes if its interaction cannot be told apart from a person's, even an unintelligent one. It says nothing about accuracy, insight or problem-solving.

stem: Select all three senses this course gives to the 'A' in 'AI'.
choices: Artifact or artifice — a machine creation made by humans
Autonomous — operating without any human supervision
Artificial semblance — when 'seems about right' will do
Adaptive — retuning its parameters as new data arrives
Artful creation — 'truth manufactured' by whatever is trending
explanation: The three A's are artifact/artifice, artificial semblance, and artful creation. Autonomy and adaptivity are real properties of AI systems but they are not what the letter A stands for here.

stem: An image generator produces a plausible-looking but entirely invented photograph. Which sense of the 'A' in 'AI' does that best illustrate?
choices: Artifact — it was built by human engineers rather than found in nature
Autonomy — it ran without a human in the loop
Artificial semblance — the output only has to seem about right
Accuracy — it matches a verifiable ground truth
explanation: Artificial semblance is the sense in which 'seems about right' is the whole standard. Artifact is true of every AI system and so does not distinguish this case, and accuracy against ground truth is the predictive-AI standard, not the generative one.

stem: What is the difference between GAI and AGI?
choices: GAI is the hardware layer; AGI is the software layer built on top of it
GAI is Generative AI, which creates new content; AGI is Artificial General Intelligence, human-level breadth across tasks
GAI is Artificial General Intelligence; AGI is Generative AI — the acronyms are simply written in different orders
GAI is any AI trained on data; AGI is any AI written as hand-coded rules
explanation: The G in GAI is Generative; the G in AGI is General. Generative AI creates new content, while Artificial General Intelligence means human-level breadth and is explicitly out of scope for this course.

stem: There are two different 'generatives' behind the G in today's GAI. Which pair names them?
choices: Generative grammar and generative design
Generative programming and generative art
Generative modelling of a data distribution, and the Generative Adversarial Network that gave the word its modern currency
Generative pre-training and generative fine-tuning
explanation: One G is generative modelling — learning a distribution so you can sample new instances. The other is Goodfellow's Generative Adversarial Network, which is where the word 'generative' entered popular use before GPT took it over.

stem: Predictive AI and generative AI are judged by different standards. Which pairing is correct?
choices: Predictive AI is judged on accuracy against verifiable ground truths; generative AI on plausible context relevance
Predictive AI is judged on plausible context relevance; generative AI on accuracy against verifiable ground truths
Both are judged on accuracy against verifiable ground truths, but generative AI is allowed a wider tolerance
Neither can be judged, because both produce outputs no one has seen before
explanation: Predictive AI is scored on accuracy against verifiable ground truths, as an MLP classifier is. Generative AI is scored on its ability to produce a response with a high degree of plausible context relevance, as GPT is.

stem: In the 'instinct to imagination' framing, predictive intelligence asks 'What WILL be?'. What does generative intelligence ask?
choices: 'What was?' — reconstructing the past from present evidence
'What is?' — classifying the situation in front of it
'What should be?' — choosing the ethically preferable outcome
'What COULD be?' — abstracting the structure of a domain and imagining plausible new instances
explanation: Predictive asks 'what WILL be' — from many throws, abstract the law of motion and predict where the ball lands. Generative asks 'what COULD be' — from many faces, abstract the essence of faceness and imagine a new one.

stem: 'Learn x to y, then crank the input' summarises predictive AI. What is the matching one-line summary of generative AI?
choices: Learn y to x, then invert the function analytically
Learn z to x, then crank the pseudo-random number generator
Learn x to y, then crank the output backwards through the network
Learn x to x, then keep cranking until the reconstruction is exact
explanation: A generative model learns a map from a simple distribution z to data x; generation means sampling z from the PRNG and pushing it through the learned map. Randomness supplies the variation, and the learned map supplies the structure.

stem: In this course's vocabulary of the mind, recognition is an interpolative map. What kind of map is generation?
choices: An iterative map, repeating the same step until it converges
A bijective map, because every output has exactly one input
An extrapolative map, into territory that was never explicitly observed
A degenerate map, because several inputs give the same output
explanation: Recognition interpolates within known territory and can be checked against ground truth. Generation extrapolates into unexplored territory, which is why the course calls it imagination rather than validation.

stem: 'Generate' is unpacked into three meanings in this course. Select all three.
choices: Simulate — draw from a distributional prior
Connect — graph or network adjacency
Compress — reduce data to fewer dimensions
Create — integrated innovation
Classify — assign an item to a predefined label
explanation: Generate maps to simulate, connect and create. Compression is what the encoder half of an autoencoder does, and classification is a predictive task — neither is a meaning of 'generate'.

stem: A discriminative model learns p(y|x). What does a generative model learn?
choices: p(x), or p(x|c) when the generation is conditioned on something
p(y), the distribution of labels on their own
The inverse function x = f-inverse(y), computed exactly
Nothing probabilistic — it memorises the training set and replays it
explanation: Discriminative modelling gives the probability of a label given an input, p(y|x). Generative modelling gives the distribution of the data itself, p(x), or p(x|c) when conditioned on a prompt or class.

stem: What does the claim 'ML builds AI' actually mean?
choices: Machine learning is a subfield of AI, so every ML result is also an AI result
Machine learning supplies the training data that AI engineers then hand-code into rules
AI cannot be programmed with traditional if-then constructs, so it is instead programmed to calibrate its model parameters from data — which is a machine-learning algorithm
Machine learning builds the hardware that AI models are trained on
explanation: The point is that intelligence cannot be pre-programmed as if-then rules; the parameters have to be calibrated from data, and that calibration is machine learning. Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning are its three principal paradigms.

stem: In what way is machine learning larger than artificial intelligence?
choices: ML is faster, so it can process more data in the same time
ML methods calibrate parameters from data in fields far outside AI — statistics, optimisation, forecasting, any data-driven modelling
ML includes rule-based expert systems, which AI does not
ML covers both software and robotics, while AI covers software only
explanation: ML is a generalisation of algorithmic parameter calibration, so it reaches into statistics, optimisation and forecasting that nobody would call AI. The trap is assuming one field simply contains the other.

stem: In what way is artificial intelligence larger than machine learning?
choices: AI has more parameters, so it can represent more complicated functions
AI includes deep learning, which is not part of machine learning
AI is a commercial category while ML is an academic one
AI also includes rule-based symbolic systems, search, planning and robotics that involve no learning from data at all
explanation: GOFAI expert systems, search and planning are AI and contain no learning whatsoever, so AI reaches outside ML. Neither field contains the other; they overlap.

stem: Select the three principal machine-learning paradigms named in this course.
choices: Adversarial learning
Supervised learning
Unsupervised learning
Federated learning
Reinforcement learning
explanation: Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement learning are the three principal paradigms, with representation learning added as a fourth modality in the course glossary. Adversarial training is a technique used inside a GAN, not a paradigm in this list.

stem: A retailer groups its customers into segments without ever being told what the correct segments are. Which learning paradigm is that, and which predictive-AI example from the course matches it?
choices: Unsupervised learning — cluster analysis, which gives segmentation insights rather than predictions against labels
Supervised learning — a multilayer perceptron trained on labelled targets
Reinforcement learning — a policy optimised against a reward signal
Generative learning — a transformer sampling plausible customer descriptions
explanation: No labels are supplied, so the structure has to come from the data itself: unsupervised learning, exemplified by cluster analysis. An MLP classifier would be the supervised example of predictive AI.

stem: Define 'valenced feeling and graded sensation' as an element of an intelligent being.
choices: The ability to report in words what it is currently sensing
Evaluating sensed input on a preferential scale from very negative to very positive, which feeds back into the learning algorithm and conditions future behaviour
The physical body and sensor array that lets an agent explore its environment
A momentary awareness of which computation step is being performed
explanation: Valence is the preferential scale — negative through neutral to positive — placed on what is sensed, and it matters because it is the feedback signal that shapes later behaviour. The body is corporal form; step awareness is the consciousness marker.

stem: Select all of the following that are elements of the course's five-part Intelligent Being.
choices: Corporal form and physical embodiment
Linguistic competence and grammar parsing
Cognitive faculty and pattern recognition
Mental formation and projective generation
Economic agency and resource ownership
explanation: The five are corporal form, valenced feeling, cognitive faculty, mental formation and consciousness marker. Language competence is an AI task, not an element of the being, and economic agency is not in the framework at all.

stem: Which two elements of the Intelligent Being correspond to predictive AI and generative AI respectively?
choices: Corporal form for predictive, valenced feeling for generative
Valenced feeling for predictive, consciousness marker for generative
Cognitive faculty and pattern recognition for predictive; mental formation and projective generation for generative
Consciousness marker for predictive, corporal form for generative
explanation: Predictive AI mimics element (iii), cognition and pattern recognition; generative AI mimics element (iv), mental formation and projective generation. That is the framework's whole reason for existing.

stem: Why does 'corporal form and physical embodiment' matter for an artificial intelligence, according to this course?
choices: It makes the system faster, because computation happens close to the sensors
It is the only way to give a system a valenced scale of feeling
It proves the system is conscious rather than merely reactive
A body with sensors and some autonomy lets the agent interactively explore its environment and learn from that interaction
explanation: Embodiment is about the loop between acting and sensing: without a body you cannot learn to swim, and without eyes you cannot learn colour. It is not a claim about speed or about consciousness.

stem: A student has ChatGPT write her essay, prepare her pitch and summarise her reading. In this course's vocabulary, what is that?
choices: Artificial Literacy — the failure mode of AI Literacy, outsourcing the thinking rather than learning to code, safeguard and explore
AI Literacy — using the tool fluently is exactly what literacy means
Artificial Application — relying on agentic AI to run content channels
Integrated Innovation — combining several capabilities into one workflow
explanation: AI Literacy means you can code, can safeguard, and can explore or exploit the technology. Artificial Literacy is the ironic opposite: leaning on the model so the competence never forms. Artificial Application is the same failure applied to agentic tools, not to study.

stem: What was the 'hard part' about applied mathematics, in the sense this course uses the word 'applied'?
choices: The mathematics itself is more advanced than in theoretical work
You have to implement everything in code rather than on paper
The conclusion has to conform to real-world constraints, which is why applied is harder than theoretical rather than simpler
Applied mathematics uses approximations, so the answers are always slightly wrong
explanation: Applied does not mean simplified. It means the result must hold under the constraints of the real situation you operate in, and that is exactly what makes it harder than the theoretical version.

stem: One word: what do you call a new name given to an older thing because a newer thing has taken over the original name — as when expert systems became 'GOFAI'?
explanation: A retronym. Expert systems were simply called AI until neural approaches claimed the name, so they were renamed Good Old-Fashioned AI; the same move renamed ordinary AI as 'predictive AI' once generative AI arrived.

stem: This course groups everything neural networks do into three function modes. Which set is correct?
choices: Training, validation and testing
Encoding, decoding and sampling
Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement
Prediction, representation and generation
explanation: Prediction, representation and generation are the three function modes, and they are the spine of the six-architecture story: MLP and CNN predict, VAE and U-Net represent, Transformer and Diffusion generate. Supervised, unsupervised and reinforcement are learning paradigms, a different axis.

stem: What does the G in 'GAI' stand for?
explanation: Generative. GAI is Generative Artificial Intelligence, which creates new content; the G in AGI is General, meaning human-level breadth across tasks, and that is explicitly outside this course.

stem: One word completes the second element of the Intelligent Being: '____ feeling and graded sensation'.
explanation: Valenced. It means grading what is sensed on a preferential scale from very negative through neutral to very positive, which then acts as feedback to the learning algorithm and conditions future behaviour.

stem: Modern deep learning is summarised in this course as five enduring principles. Which set is right, in order?
choices: Data, Model, Training, Evaluation, Deployment
Representation, Relation, Parameterization, Optimization, Architecture
Perception, Memory, Reasoning, Planning, Action
Encoding, Compression, Sampling, Decoding, Generation
explanation: Represent, relate, parameterize, learn, orchestrate. Every seminal paper on the course's list contributes to one or more of the five, and the later ones contribute to several at once.

stem: One word: the first of the five principles of modern deep learning, which turns information into vectors or tensors so that it becomes computable.
explanation: Representation: information becomes numerical representation. Tokens and embeddings for text, patches and tensors for images — nothing else in the pipeline can run until the data are numbers.

stem: Which of the five principles of modern deep learning is described as the clever orchestration of the other four?
choices: Representation
Optimization
Architecture
Relation
explanation: Architecture is the higher-level design that decides how representations, relations, parameterised operations and learning interact. It is why the course says intelligence comes from orchestration rather than from any single ingredient.

stem: What does this course claim the progress of deep learning actually consists of?
choices: Steadily more complicated primitive mathematics
Steadily larger datasets, with the mathematics unchanged since 1986
Increasingly ingenious orchestration of representations, relationships, parameters and learning, rather than more complicated primitive mathematics
The replacement of statistics by a genuinely new branch of mathematics
explanation: The primitives stay simple: a weighted sum, a nonlinearity, a derivative. What changes is how ingeniously they are arranged, which is the claim the five principles are there to support.

stem: Attention, with its queries, keys and values, is offered as the textbook example of which principle?
choices: Relation — expressing abstract relationships as operations among representations
Representation — encoding information as vectors
Optimization — making the system differentiable
Parameterization — many simple operations composed
explanation: Attention is a relation: it computes how strongly each representation should bear on each other one. Embedding is the representation step that must happen first, which is exactly the embedding-versus-attention distinction in another form.

stem: 'Simple operations, massively parameterized and composed, can express complex functions.' Which principle is that?
choices: Representation
Relation
Optimization
Parameterization
explanation: Parameterization: complexity is bought with learned parameters and composition, not with exotic mathematics. It is the principle that makes a 175-billion-parameter model a difference of degree rather than of kind.

stem: In the five-principle scheme, what does making a system differentiable buy you?
choices: It guarantees the global minimum will be found
It makes the network's decisions interpretable
It removes the need for a loss function
It lets the numerical parameters be learned from data by gradient-based methods
explanation: Differentiability is the precondition for optimization, the fourth principle: no derivative, no gradient, no learning. It says nothing about whether the minimum found is the best one.

stem: The Transformer is credited against all five principles at once, where most earlier work touches only one or two. Why?
choices: Because it is the most recent architecture on the list
Because it has more parameters than anything before it

Because it re-represents tokens as embeddings, expresses relation through attention, is massively parameterised, is trained end to end by gradient descent, and its actual contribution is the orchestration of all four
Because it can be used for both text and images
explanation: The Transformer is an architecture in the strict sense of the fifth principle: a way of arranging the other four. That is the reason it generalised from translation to language, vision, audio and code.

stem: The course's literacy roadmap runs through four stages. Which are they, in order?
choices: Words, timelines, how it works under the hood, application
Mathematics, code, architecture, deployment
History, ethics, regulation, practice
Data, model, evaluation, impact
explanation: Build the language first, then the history, then the mechanisms, then what you can do with it. The order is deliberate: you cannot ask how a thing works until you can name its parts.

stem: The roadmap names three complementary families of timeline rather than one. Which set is right?
choices: Language, vision and audio
Academic, commercial and military
Task equivalence, computational model, and integrated autonomy
Hardware, software and data
explanation: Task-equivalence timelines track reproducing human capabilities; computational-model timelines track competing conceptions of intelligence; integrated-autonomy timelines track the move from models to real-world agency. They are complementary views, not a strict taxonomy.

stem: The integrated-autonomy timeline runs from AI as software to what?
choices: AI as a service, then AI as a subscription
AI as an operating system, meaning agentic AI with reasoning, planning and tool use, and then AI as hardware, meaning robotics and embodied AI
AI as a search engine, then AI as a database
AI as a compiler, then AI as an interpreter
explanation: Software means predictive then generative models; operating system means the agentic layer that plans and calls tools; hardware means a physical agent acting in the world. That last rung is where the Intelligent Being's corporal form becomes the topic.

stem: Chatbot, RAG, agent and wiki are distinguished by one verb each. Which set is right?
choices: Talks with you, searches for you, does things for you, builds your knowledge
Answers for you, writes for you, decides for you, remembers for you
Chats with you, thinks for you, sells to you, teaches you
Explains to you, retrieves for you, argues with you, stores for you
explanation: A chatbot talks with you, RAG searches for you with grounded references, an agent does things for you through tool use and multi-step execution, and a wiki accumulates knowledge with you. Four words that cover the whole application layer.

stem: One word: the application mode that does things for you, through tool use, workflow automation and multi-step task execution.
explanation: An agent. The distinction worth holding: a chatbot talks with you, RAG searches for you, an agent does things for you, and a wiki builds knowledge with you.

stem: Select all three senses this course gives to the 'I' in 'AI'.
choices: Human-like, as in 'the most intelligent being' — the sense Turing's imitation game tests
Instinctive, as in a reflex that needs no learning
Advantageous information of strategic or tactical value, as in military or business intelligence
Immutable, as in a rule that cannot be retrained
A solution path or method for a hard problem, as in computational or digital intelligence
explanation: Human-like, advantageous information, and optimal solution method. Being able to name at least three forms of intelligence was flagged in class; the trap is to give only the first, which is the one everybody thinks of.

stem: Asked to name at least three forms of intelligence, which set would this course accept?
choices: Artificial, natural and hybrid
Human-like intelligence; intelligence as advantageous information; computational or digital intelligence as an optimal solution
Narrow, general and super
Predictive, generative and adversarial
explanation: Three different words wearing one label. The imitation game tests the first, a business dashboard delivers the second, and an optimisation algorithm delivers the third — and only the first is about behaving like a person.

stem: An AI system is intelligent but cannot do anything in the world; a robot can do things but is not intelligent. What is the term for what you get by joining the two?
choices: Artificial general intelligence
Reinforcement learning
Embodied AI — a physical form with the ability to experience and act in its environment
Agentic workflow
explanation: Embodied AI is the rung where a model acquires a body and sensors, so it can explore and learn from an environment rather than only process what it is handed. It is the reason corporal form is the first element of the Intelligent Being.

stem: 'Being hungry is not an intelligent calculation — it is reading a negative signal coming from the body.' Which element of the Intelligent Being does that illustrate?
choices: Cognitive faculty and pattern recognition
Valenced feeling and graded sensation
Mental formation and projective generation
Consciousness marker and program register
explanation: Valenced feeling and graded sensation: the being categorises its sensations as positive, negative or neutral, by degree. It is not reasoning — it is a signal with a sign attached, and that sign is what drives the being to act.

stem: A computer scientist and a data scientist describe the relation between AI and machine learning in opposite directions. How?
choices: To the computer scientist, machine learning sits inside AI as one of the things AI research encompasses; to the data scientist, AI is the packaging and branding placed on top of machine learning
To the computer scientist, AI is a subfield of statistics; to the data scientist, it is a subfield of robotics
Both place machine learning inside AI; the disagreement is only about which is older
Neither uses the term machine learning; they both say AI
explanation: Two professions looking at the same stack from opposite ends, which is why the containment question has no single answer. The course's own version: neither contains the other — ML reaches outside AI into any data-driven calibration, and AI reaches outside ML into symbolic systems, search and planning.

stem: 'All fiction is realistic but not real.' How does that sentence separate generative AI from predictive AI?
choices: It does not — both produce fiction
Predictive AI produces fiction and generative AI produces fact
Predictive AI approximates reality and is checked against it; generative AI takes what it has learned and runs with it, producing something realistic that was never real
Generative AI copies real examples while predictive AI invents new ones
explanation: Approximating reality is prediction; taking a learned structure and running with it is generation. The consequence for marking is that a generative output cannot be scored against a ground truth — only for plausibility.
